sentences.context: Ask four of the world's biggest university rankings who is #1 and you get four different answers.
sentences.summary: ana_06: The four tables crown four different champions (ranking, strong). Data: the/timesData.csv, arwu/shanghaiData.csv, qs/QS_2023_Dataset.csv, cwur/cwurData.csv, openalex/openalex_institutions_research_output.csv, leiden/leiden_open_2024_universities.xlsx, _join/school_and_country_table.csv. Built on det_08, det_13. | det_08: The systems correlate weakly and crown different winners. Source: Relationship between bibliometric indicators and university ranking positions (PMC) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10468493/) Facts: Rankings are statistically correlated yet show many cases of high divergence and instability; Reconciliation schemes yield correlations in the narrow 0.7-0.8 range for Times, QS and Shanghai Source: A Longitudinal Analysis of University Rankings (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.10632) Facts: Documents year-to-year instability in the major global ranking systems Source: How Reliable are University Rankings? (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.09006) Facts: Critically examines the reliability and reproducibility of the major ranking methodologies

raw_evidence.label: The systems correlate weakly and crown different winners
raw_evidence.content: Academic studies confirm the core premise: the big systems are statistically correlated but diverge sharply for individual universities and are unstable year to year. Reconciliation studies find pairwise rank correlations only in the 0.7-0.8 range for Times/QS/Shanghai, with 'many cases of high divergence and instability'. The disagreement even reaches the very top — in recent editions no single university leads all three (MIT tops QS, Oxford tops THE, Harvard tops ARWU), and this dataset's own years already disagree on #1 (ARWU 2015 and CWUR 2015 crown Harvard, THE 2015 crowns Caltech, QS 2023 crowns MIT). That the tables can't even agree who is best is the clearest evidence that 'best' is a weighting choice.

Reconciliation schemes yield correlations in the narrow 0.7-0.8 range for Times, QS and Shanghai
Absolute publication/citation counts dominate ARWU while field-weighted citation impact is central to THE

raw_evidence.label: The four tables crown four different champions
raw_evidence.content: The disagreement reaches the very #1 spot. THE 2015 crowns Caltech, ARWU 2015 and CWUR 2015 crown Harvard, QS 2023 crowns MIT — and the neutral OpenAlex output order crowns yet another school, University of Michigan. Only five universities (Harvard, Stanford, MIT, Cambridge, Oxford) appear in ALL FOUR commercial top-10s, out of 15 distinct names that appear in any top-10; the other ten seats are contested (Caltech, Princeton, Berkeley, Imperial, Yale, Columbia, Chicago, Cornell, UCL, ETH Zurich). The side-by-side top-10 is the opening 'they can't even agree who's best' table.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_06: each system's TOP 10 side by side (different #1, different membership) ---
print("=== ana_06 ===")
the = c.load_the(); arwu = c.load_arwu(); cwur = c.load_cwur(); qs = c.load_qs(); oa = c.load_openalex()
def top10(df, namecol, ranksort):
    return df.sort_values(ranksort).head(10)[namecol].tolist()
t10 = {
    "THE 2015": top10(the, "university_name", "rank_num"),
    "ARWU 2015": top10(arwu, "university_name", "rank_num"),
    "CWUR 2015": top10(cwur, "institution", "rank_num"),
    "QS 2023": top10(qs, "institution", "rank_num"),
    "OpenAlex (works)": oa.sort_values("works_count", ascending=False).head(10)["institution"].tolist(),
}
tbl = pd.DataFrame({k: v for k, v in t10.items()})
tbl.index = range(1, 11)
print(tbl.to_string())
print("\n#1 of each table:", {k: v[0] for k, v in t10.items()})
# how much do the top-10 sets overlap?
sets = {k: set(c.normalize_name(x) for x in v) for k, v in t10.items() if k != "OpenAlex (works)"}
inter = set.intersection(*sets.values())
raw_evidence.output:
#1 of each table: {'THE 2015': 'California Institute of Technology', 'ARWU 2015': 'Harvard University', 'CWUR 2015': 'Harvard University', 'QS 2023': 'Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)', 'OpenAlex (works)': 'University of Michigan'}
Universities in ALL FOUR commercial top-10s: 5 of 15 distinct names

Source: University rankings: A review of methodological flaws (https://iier.org.au/iier30/fauzi.pdf) Facts: Reviews systematic methodological flaws in global rankings, including reputation-survey bias toward established, well-known institutions and the sensitivity of results to normalisation and weighting choices Source: Relationship between bibliometric indicators and university ranking positions (PMC) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10468493/) Facts: Absolute publication and citation COUNTS drive ARWU/U.S. News, whereas field-weighted (normalised) citation impact drives THE — so raw-volume and normalised metrics rank the same universities differently

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook — the prestige loop and the size effect
raw_evidence.content: Two mechanisms explain most of the disagreement and give the story its characters. First, reputation surveys create a self-reinforcing prestige (halo) loop that favours older, larger, English-speaking, already-famous universities — so QS's survey-heavy order rewards name recognition, which is partly downstream of past rankings. Second, normalisation choices flip the winners: THE and QS divide citations by faculty, so a tiny, citation-dense, science-focused school like Caltech can top THE, while a metric based on RAW output volume (OpenAlex works_count) instead crowns sprawling multi-faculty, medical-heavy giants like the University of Michigan or Toronto that no commercial table places first. The same universities therefore swing tens of places between systems purely because of what is weighted and whether it is size-normalised — Caltech (small, normalised winner) and Michigan (large, raw-volume winner) are the perfect two-sided illustration.

Source: QS World University Rankings (Wikipedia) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QS_World_University_Rankings) Facts: In the 2017 QS International Student Survey, 23.5% said institutional ranking was the most important factor in choosing a university and subject, and 19.6% said rankings were important in choosing a country of study Source: Rankings and the Reshaping of Higher Education (Hazelkorn) (https://link.springer.com/book/10.1057/9781137446671) Facts: Rankings influence students, parents, governments, funding agencies, employers and public opinion, reshaping higher education in the age of globalisation

raw_evidence.label: Why it matters — rankings steer real decisions
raw_evidence.content: These tables are not academic parlour games; they move students, money and policy. In QS's own International Student Survey, roughly a quarter of prospective students (23.5%) said institutional ranking was the single most important factor in choosing a university and subject, and about a fifth (19.6%) said rankings shaped which COUNTRY they studied in. Ellen Hazelkorn's landmark work documents how rankings now reshape decisions not just for students and parents but for governments, funding agencies, employers and universities' own strategies — a 'global reputation race' in which a few weighting choices by three or four private companies ripple into national policy and billions in tuition and research funding. That stakes-per-decision is exactly why the disagreement between the tables is worth exposing.

Ellen Hazelkorn's landmark work documents how rankings now reshape decisions not just for students and parents but for governments, funding agencies, employers and universities' own strategies — a 'global reputation race' in which a few weighting choices by three or four private companies ripple into national policy and billions in tuition and research funding. That stakes-per-decision is exactly why the disagreement between the tables is worth exposing.

raw_evidence.label: The systems correlate weakly and crown different winners
raw_evidence.content: Academic studies confirm the core premise: the big systems are statistically correlated but diverge sharply for individual universities and are unstable year to year. Reconciliation studies find pairwise rank correlations only in the 0.7-0.8 range for Times/QS/Shanghai, with 'many cases of high divergence and instability'. The disagreement even reaches the very top — in recent editions no single university leads all three (MIT tops QS, Oxford tops THE, Harvard tops ARWU), and this dataset's own years already disagree on #1 (ARWU 2015 and CWUR 2015 crown Harvard, THE 2015 crowns Caltech, QS 2023 crowns MIT). That the tables can't even agree who is best is the clearest evidence that 'best' is a weighting choice.

raw_evidence.label: The 4 systems correlate only 0.60-0.85 (Spearman)
raw_evidence.content: On the 218-school common core, the six pairwise rank correlations between the commercial systems span Spearman 0.599 to 0.853 (Kendall 0.426 to 0.706) — 'correlated but far from agreeing', exactly the 0.7-0.8 band the literature reports (det_08). The two most alike are ARWU and CWUR (Spearman 0.853) — unsurprising, since both are survey-free research tables. The two LEAST alike are CWUR and QS (0.599), and QS's other two pairings are also the weakest (QS-ARWU 0.647, QS-THE 0.735): QS, the reputation-survey pole, is the systematic outlier. NB QS's low correlations partly reflect its 2023 edition vs the others' 2015 (see ana_11).
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_04: pairwise rank correlations among the 4 commercial systems ---
print("=== ana_04 ===")
rows = []
for i in range(len(SYS)):
    for j in range(i + 1, len(SYS)):
        a, b = SYS[i], SYS[j]
        sub = m[[a, b]].dropna()
        rho, _ = spearmanr(sub[a], sub[b])
        tau, _ = kendalltau(sub[a], sub[b])
        rows.append((LAB[a], LAB[b], len(sub), round(rho, 3), round(tau, 3)))
        print(f"{LAB[a]:>4} vs {LAB[b]:<4}  n={len(sub):3d}  Spearman={rho:.3f}  Kendall={tau:.3f}")
rows_sorted = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r[3])
print("MOST alike pair (highest Spearman):", rows_sorted[-1][:2], rows_sorted[-1][3])
print("LEAST alike pair (lowest Spearman):", rows_sorted[0][:2], rows_sorted[0][3])
print("Spearman range across the 6 pairs: %.3f to %.3f" % (rows_sorted[0][3], rows_sorted[-1][3]))

raw_evidence.label: The systems correlate weakly and crown different winners
raw_evidence.content: Academic studies confirm the core premise: the big systems are statistically correlated but diverge sharply for individual universities and are unstable year to year. Reconciliation studies find pairwise rank correlations only in the 0.7-0.8 range for Times/QS/Shanghai, with 'many cases of high divergence and instability'. The disagreement even reaches the very top — in recent editions no single university leads all three (MIT tops QS, Oxford tops THE, Harvard tops ARWU), and this dataset's own years already disagree on #1 (ARWU 2015 and CWUR 2015 crown Harvard, THE 2015 crowns Caltech, QS 2023 crowns MIT). That the tables can't even agree who is best is the clearest evidence that 'best' is a weighting choice.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook — the prestige loop and the size effect
raw_evidence.content: Two mechanisms explain most of the disagreement and give the story its characters. First, reputation surveys create a self-reinforcing prestige (halo) loop that favours older, larger, English-speaking, already-famous universities — so QS's survey-heavy order rewards name recognition, which is partly downstream of past rankings. Second, normalisation choices flip the winners: THE and QS divide citations by faculty, so a tiny, citation-dense, science-focused school like Caltech can top THE, while a metric based on RAW output volume (OpenAlex works_count) instead crowns sprawling multi-faculty, medical-heavy giants like the University of Michigan or Toronto that no commercial table places first. The same universities therefore swing tens of places between systems purely because of what is weighted and whether it is size-normalised — Caltech (small, normalised winner) and Michigan (large, raw-volume winner) are the perfect two-sided illustration.

raw_evidence.label: QS methodology — the reputation-survey pole
raw_evidence.content: QS is the most reputation-driven of the four systems. In the pre-2024 methodology used for the 2023 edition in this dataset, Academic Reputation (a global survey of academics) was worth 40% and Employer Reputation (a survey of employers) 10% — so surveyed opinion alone drove HALF of a university's QS score. The remaining weight was split between Citations per Faculty (20%, research impact from Elsevier Scopus), Faculty/Student Ratio (20%, a teaching-capacity proxy) and international faculty + student share (5% each). Reputation responses are pooled over a rolling five-year window. This is why QS is the natural counter-pole to ARWU: its order is dominated by perception, not measured output.

facts: Academic Reputation 40%, Employer Reputation 10%, Citations per Faculty 20%, Faculty/Student Ratio 20%, International Faculty 5%, International Students 5% (pre-2024 methodology)
Citations-per-faculty data is drawn from Elsevier Scopus
The reputation surveys pool responses over the previous five years

raw_evidence.label: BENCHMARK — how much each table is reputation vs measured output
raw_evidence.content: The single most useful comparison for the Analyst is the reputation-vs-output weighting of each system, because it is the mechanical reason they disagree. Reputation-survey share of the total score: QS ~50% (Academic 40% + Employer 10%); THE ~33% (15% teaching survey + 18% research survey) but with a further 30% on citations; ARWU 0% (100% research output + elite prizes); CWUR 0% (surveys are excluded by design). OpenAlex is 0% reputation by construction — it is raw output/impact only. So along a 'perception ↔ measured output' axis the four systems fan out from QS (most perception) through THE to ARWU/CWUR (most output), with OpenAlex as the pure-output anchor beyond them.

raw_evidence.label: THE methodology — reputation + citations blend
raw_evidence.content: Times Higher Education blends performance and reputation. For the 2011-2023 editions (the family the 2011-2016 data here belongs to) THE used five pillars weighted Teaching 30%, Research 30%, Citations 30%, International outlook 7.5% and Industry income 2.5%. Reputation surveys are baked INSIDE the Teaching and Research pillars — 15% of the overall score from the teaching reputation survey plus 18% from the research reputation survey, i.e. about a third of the total is still surveyed opinion. But unlike QS, THE also gives fully 30% to field-normalised Citations (research influence), which is what lets citation-dense small institutions like Caltech top the table. THE later replaced this structure with 'WUR 3.0' in 2024.

raw_evidence.label: ARWU methodology — pure research & elite prizes
raw_evidence.content: ARWU (the Shanghai Ranking), first published in 2003 by Shanghai Jiao Tong University and since 2009 by ShanghaiRanking Consultancy, is almost purely a research-and-prizes machine with NO reputation survey and NO teaching pillar. Its six indicators are: Alumni winning Nobel Prizes / Fields Medals (10%), Staff winning Nobel Prizes / Fields Medals (20%), Highly Cited Researchers per Clarivate (20%), papers in Nature & Science (20%), papers indexed in SCIE/SSCI (20%), and per-capita academic performance (10%). Because half the score rides on elite prizes and highly-cited-researcher counts, ARWU rewards a very different profile from QS — a university can sit top-5 in ARWU and middling in QS.

raw_evidence.label: CWUR methodology — outcomes + research, no surveys
raw_evidence.content: The Center for World University Rankings (CWUR) is distinctive because it uses NO reputation surveys and NO university-submitted data at all, relying only on independently verifiable indicators — which is exactly what makes it a useful 'commercial-but-not-survey-based' tiebreaker. Its current scheme groups seven indicators into four areas: Education 25% (alumni academic success relative to size), Employability 25% (alumni professional success), Faculty 10% (top academic distinctions) and Research 40% (output, high-quality publications, and influence/citations). Note: the 2012-2015 editions in THIS dataset use an OLDER eight-indicator version whose columns are RANKS (1 = best), not 0-100 scores — quality of education, alumni employment, quality of faculty, publications, influence, citations, broad impact and patents.

raw_evidence.label: THE methodology — reputation + citations blend
raw_evidence.content: Times Higher Education blends performance and reputation. For the 2011-2023 editions (the family the 2011-2016 data here belongs to) THE used five pillars weighted Teaching 30%, Research 30%, Citations 30%, International outlook 7.5% and Industry income 2.5%. But unlike QS, THE also gives fully 30% to field-normalised Citations (research influence), which is what lets citation-dense small institutions like Caltech top the table. THE later replaced this structure with 'WUR 3.0' in 2024.

raw_evidence.content: ARWU (the Shanghai Ranking), first published in 2003 by Shanghai Jiao Tong University and since 2009 by ShanghaiRanking Consultancy, is almost purely a research-and-prizes machine with NO reputation survey and NO teaching pillar. raw_evidence.label: QS methodology — the reputation-survey pole
raw_evidence.content: QS is the most reputation-driven of the four systems. In the pre-2024 methodology used for the 2023 edition in this dataset, Academic Reputation (a global survey of academics) was worth 40% and Employer Reputation (a survey of employers) 10% — so surveyed opinion alone drove HALF of a university's QS score. The remaining weight was split between Citations per Faculty (20%, research impact from Elsevier Scopus), Faculty/Student Ratio (20%, a teaching-capacity proxy) and international faculty + student share (5% each). Reputation responses are pooled over a rolling five-year window. This is why QS is the natural counter-pole to ARWU: its order is dominated by perception, not measured output.

sources.title: Understanding the Methodology: QS World University Rankings (TopUniversities)
facts: Academic Reputation 40%, Employer Reputation 10%, Citations per Faculty 20%, Faculty/Student Ratio 20%, International Faculty 5%, International Students 5% (pre-2024 methodology)
Citations-per-faculty data is drawn from Elsevier Scopus
The reputation surveys pool responses over the previous five years

raw_evidence.label: Reputation vs research — the survey lifts different schools
raw_evidence.content: Within QS itself, the Academic-Reputation survey score and the Citations-per-Faculty score correlate only Spearman 0.421 across the 218 core — the survey and the citation metric rank schools very differently. Comparing QS to ARWU on schools both rank <=200: QS lifts reputation-rich Asia-Pacific names far above ARWU's research-and-prizes order — University of Hong Kong (ARWU 151 / QS 21), NUS (101/11), Peking (101/12), Tsinghua (101/14), Seoul National (101/29). The reverse (ARWU >> QS) lifts US research-heavy schools — Vanderbilt (ARWU 53 / QS 199), Maryland (43/164), UCSB (38/149), Florida (83/188), WashU St Louis (32/118). Inside QS's own indicators, its reputation metric most over-lifts famous names with thin per-faculty citations (NYU AR 95.9 / CPF 28.9; Toronto 99.6 / 43.5; TU Munich 84.0 / 25.8), while its citation metric lifts research-dense but less-famous schools (Dartmouth AR 19.2 / CPF 86.7; Rensselaer 8.4 / 70.5; Bern 30.3 / 98.3).
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_09: reputation-lifted vs research-lifted (QS vs ARWU rank gap + QS sub-scores) ---
print("=== ana_09 ===")
m["qs_minus_arwu"] = m["qs_rank"] - m["arwu_rank"]   # negative => QS ranks it HIGHER (reputation lift)
cols = ["the_name", "country", "arwu_rank", "qs_rank", "qs_minus_arwu", "ar score", "cpf score", "oa_rank_works"]
clean = m[(m["arwu_rank"] <= 200) & (m["qs_rank"] <= 200)].copy()
print("(clean cut: both ARWU and QS rank <=200, %d schools, avoids tail-band artefacts)" % len(clean))
print("REPUTATION-LIFTED (QS ranks far ABOVE ARWU; survey opinion > measured research):")
print(clean.sort_values("qs_minus_arwu").head(10)[cols].to_string(index=False))
print("\nRESEARCH-LIFTED (ARWU ranks far ABOVE QS; measured research > reputation):")
print(clean.sort_values("qs_minus_arwu", ascending=False).head(10)[cols].to_string(index=False))
# QS's own internal split: Academic Reputation vs Citations-per-Faculty
sub = m.dropna(subset=["ar score", "cpf score"]).copy()
sub["ar_rank"] = sub["ar score"].rank(ascending=False, method="min")
sub["cpf_rank"] = sub["cpf score"].rank(ascending=False, method="min")
sub["ar_minus_cpf"] = sub["ar_rank"] - sub["cpf_rank"]   # positive => citations rank it higher than reputation
from scipy.stats import spearmanr  # noqa: E402
r, _ = spearmanr(sub["ar score"], sub["cpf score"])
print("\nWithin QS itself, Academic-Reputation score vs Citations-per-Faculty score correlate only Spearman=%.3f "
      "(n=%d) — the survey and the citation metric rank schools differently." % (r, len(sub)))
print("Schools QS's CITATION metric lifts most over its REPUTATION metric (research-dense, low name-recognition):")
print(sub.sort_values("ar_minus_cpf", ascending=False).head(6)[
    ["the_name", "ar score", "cpf score"]].to_string(index=False))
print("Schools QS's REPUTATION metric lifts most over its CITATION metric (famous name, thinner per-faculty citations):")
print(sub.sort_values("ar_minus_cpf").head(6)[
    ["the_name", "ar score", "cpf score"]].to_string(index=False))

Source: University rankings: A review of methodological flaws (https://iier.org.au/iier30/fauzi.pdf) Facts: Reviews systematic methodological flaws in global rankings, including reputation-survey bias toward established, well-known institutions and the sensitivity of results to normalisation and weighting choices Source: Relationship between bibliometric indicators and university ranking positions (PMC) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10468493/) Facts: Absolute publication and citation COUNTS drive ARWU/U.S. News, whereas field-weighted (normalised) citation impact drives THE — so raw-volume and normalised metrics rank the same universities differently

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook — the prestige loop and the size effect
raw_evidence.content: Two mechanisms explain most of the disagreement and give the story its characters. First, reputation surveys create a self-reinforcing prestige (halo) loop that favours older, larger, English-speaking, already-famous universities — so QS's survey-heavy order rewards name recognition, which is partly downstream of past rankings. Second, normalisation choices flip the winners: THE and QS divide citations by faculty, so a tiny, citation-dense, science-focused school like Caltech can top THE, while a metric based on RAW output volume (OpenAlex works_count) instead crowns sprawling multi-faculty, medical-heavy giants like the University of Michigan or Toronto that no commercial table places first. The same universities therefore swing tens of places between systems purely because of what is weighted and whether it is size-normalised — Caltech (small, normalised winner) and Michigan (large, raw-volume winner) are the perfect two-sided illustration.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook — the prestige loop and the size effect
raw_evidence.content: Two mechanisms explain most of the disagreement and give the story its characters. First, reputation surveys create a self-reinforcing prestige (halo) loop that favours older, larger, English-speaking, already-famous universities — so QS's survey-heavy order rewards name recognition, which is partly downstream of past rankings. Second, normalisation choices flip the winners: THE and QS divide citations by faculty, so a tiny, citation-dense, science-focused school like Caltech can top THE, while a metric based on RAW output volume (OpenAlex works_count) instead crowns sprawling multi-faculty, medical-heavy giants like the University of Michigan or Toronto that no commercial table places first. The same universities therefore swing tens of places between systems purely because of what is weighted and whether it is size-normalised — Caltech (small, normalised winner) and Michigan (large, raw-volume winner) are the perfect two-sided illustration.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook — the prestige loop and the size effect
raw_evidence.content: Two mechanisms explain most of the disagreement and give the story its characters. First, reputation surveys create a self-reinforcing prestige (halo) loop that favours older, larger, English-speaking, already-famous universities — so QS's survey-heavy order rewards name recognition, which is partly downstream of past rankings. Second, normalisation choices flip the winners: THE and QS divide citations by faculty, so a tiny, citation-dense, science-focused school like Caltech can top THE, while a metric based on RAW output volume (OpenAlex works_count) instead crowns sprawling multi-faculty, medical-heavy giants like the University of Michigan or Toronto that no commercial table places first. The same universities therefore swing tens of places between systems purely because of what is weighted and whether it is size-normalised — Caltech (small, normalised winner) and Michigan (large, raw-volume winner) are the perfect two-sided illustration.

raw_evidence.label: OpenAlex — the neutral open research-output referee
raw_evidence.content: OpenAlex is the story's neutral yardstick: a fully open, CC0 index of scholarly works, authors and institutions launched in January 2022 by the non-profit OurResearch as the successor to Microsoft Academic Graph (which Microsoft shut down at the end of 2021). It carries metadata for 200M+ works, is free via a high-volume REST API, and is positioned as an open alternative to the commercial Scopus and Web of Science databases the ranking companies rely on. For this story it supplies an order that owes nothing to any commercial methodology — raw works_count, total cited_by_count and h_index per institution. Its coverage is not perfectly even (documented discrepancies exist, e.g. for China), which the Analyst should treat as a caveat rather than a flaw.

raw_evidence.label: The referee crowns three different winners of its own
raw_evidence.content: OpenAlex does not settle the argument — it opens a new one. Ranked by raw works_count it crowns University of Michigan; by total cited_by_count, Harvard; by h_index, University of Washington. Three neutral lenses, three different #1s, none matching Caltech/Harvard(x2)/MIT from the commercial tables (only Harvard-by-citations coincides with ARWU/CWUR). The neutral lenses even disagree with each OTHER: works vs cited_by correlate 0.873 and works vs h_index only 0.762. Michigan is the emblem — OpenAlex-works #1 but its best commercial rank is only #17 (THE): the raw-output giant no ranking table will crown.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_08: the referee crowns another order (works vs cites vs h-index) ---
print("=== ana_08 ===")
oa = c.load_openalex()
def topn(metric, n=10):
    return oa.sort_values(metric, ascending=False).head(n)[["institution", metric]].reset_index(drop=True)
w = topn("works_count"); ci = topn("cited_by_count"); h = topn("h_index")
tbl = pd.DataFrame({
    "by works_count": w["institution"], "by cited_by_count": ci["institution"], "by h_index": h["institution"],
})
tbl.index = range(1, 11)
print(tbl.to_string())
print("\nOpenAlex #1 by each lens:",
      dict(works=w.institution[0], cited_by=ci.institution[0], h_index=h.institution[0]))
# do these three neutral orders even agree at the top?
rw_c, _ = spearmanr(oa["works_count"].rank(ascending=False), oa["cited_by_count"].rank(ascending=False))
rw_h, _ = spearmanr(oa["works_count"].rank(ascending=False), oa["h_index"].rank(ascending=False))
print("Spearman among the neutral lenses themselves: works vs cited_by=%.3f, works vs h_index=%.3f "
      "(the referee disagrees with ITSELF depending on volume vs impact)." % (rw_c, rw_h))
# Michigan crown vs commercial best rank
mi = m[m.key == "michigan"].iloc[0]
print("Michigan: OpenAlex works rank #%d, but best commercial rank is #%d (THE) — the raw-output giant no table crowns."

QS tracks measured IMPACT least (0.636 vs h_index) — consistent with its 50% reputation weighting. Crucially, even the best correlation (0.88) is far from 1.0: no commercial table is 'just measuring output', so OpenAlex does not vindicate any single one.

Ranked by raw works_count it crowns University of Michigan; by total cited_by_count, Harvard; by h_index, University of Washington. Three neutral lenses, three different #1s, none matching Caltech/Harvard(x2)/MIT from the commercial tables (only Harvard-by-citations coincides with ARWU/CWUR). The neutral lenses even disagree with each OTHER: works vs cited_by correlate 0.873 and works vs h_index only 0.762. # --- ana_08: the referee crowns another order (works vs cites vs h-index) ---
print("=== ana_08 ===")
oa = c.load_openalex()
def topn(metric, n=10):
    return oa.sort_values(metric, ascending=False).head(n)[["institution", metric]].reset_index(drop=True)
w = topn("works_count"); ci = topn("cited_by_count"); h = topn("h_index")
tbl = pd.DataFrame({
    "by works_count": w["institution"], "by cited_by_count": ci["institution"], "by h_index": h["institution"],
})
tbl.index = range(1, 11)
print(tbl.to_string())
print("\nOpenAlex #1 by each lens:",
      dict(works=w.institution[0], cited_by=ci.institution[0], h_index=h.institution[0]))
# do these three neutral orders even agree at the top?

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook — the prestige loop and the size effect
raw_evidence.content: Two mechanisms explain most of the disagreement and give the story its characters. First, reputation surveys create a self-reinforcing prestige (halo) loop that favours older, larger, English-speaking, already-famous universities — so QS's survey-heavy order rewards name recognition, which is partly downstream of past rankings. Second, normalisation choices flip the winners: THE and QS divide citations by faculty, so a tiny, citation-dense, science-focused school like Caltech can top THE, while a metric based on RAW output volume (OpenAlex works_count) instead crowns sprawling multi-faculty, medical-heavy giants like the University of Michigan or Toronto that no commercial table places first. The same universities therefore swing tens of places between systems purely because of what is weighted and whether it is size-normalised — Caltech (small, normalised winner) and Michigan (large, raw-volume winner) are the perfect two-sided illustration.

raw_evidence.label: Size-normalisation flip — volume crowns Michigan, per-paper crowns Harvard
raw_evidence.content: Whether 'best research' means volume or per-paper impact flips the winner completely. By raw works_count OpenAlex crowns University of Michigan (980,174 works) but its citations-per-work is only 67.2 (impact rank #332) — a +331-place flip. Toronto flips +55 (volume #5, impact #60). At the other pole, small citation-dense schools soar when you divide by output: Caltech is volume #82 but per-paper impact #13 (-69), Princeton volume #104 / impact #24 (-80), MIT volume #35 / impact #3 (-32). Harvard is the rare school that is both big and dense (volume #2, per-paper impact #1). This is det_13's Caltech-vs-Michigan two-sided illustration, quantified: the same neutral database ranks the 'best' completely differently depending on one normalisation choice.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_10: the size-normalisation flip — volume vs per-paper impact ---
print("=== ana_10 ===")
oa = c.load_openalex()
oa = oa.copy()
oa["cites_per_work"] = oa["cited_by_count"] / oa["works_count"]
oa["rank_volume"] = oa["works_count"].rank(ascending=False, method="min").astype(int)
oa["rank_impact"] = oa["cites_per_work"].rank(ascending=False, method="min").astype(int)
oa["flip"] = oa["rank_impact"] - oa["rank_volume"]   # negative => impact rank much better than volume rank
# restrict to a meaningful set (top-120 by volume) so tiny-count outliers don't dominate per-paper
big = oa[oa["rank_volume"] <= 120].copy()
print("Top of the VOLUME order (works_count) — the sprawling giants:")
print(oa.sort_values("rank_volume").head(8)[
    ["institution", "works_count", "cites_per_work", "rank_volume", "rank_impact"]].to_string(index=False))
print("\nTop of the PER-PAPER IMPACT order (cites/work), within the top-120 by volume — the dense schools:")
print(big.sort_values("cites_per_work", ascending=False).head(8)[
    ["institution", "works_count", "cites_per_work", "rank_volume", "rank_impact"]].to_string(index=False))
# the headline flip, named
for name in ["University of Michigan", "University of Toronto", "Harvard University",
             "California Institute of Technology", "Princeton University",
             "Massachusetts Institute of Technology"]:
    row = oa[oa.institution.str.fullmatch(name, case=False, na=False)]
    if len(row):
        r0 = row.iloc[0]
        print(f"{name}: works={int(r0.works_count):>7} (volume #{int(r0.rank_volume):>3}) | "
              f"cites/work={r0.cites_per_work:5.1f} (impact #{int(r0.rank_impact):>3}) | flip {int(r0.flip):+d}")
print("Two_yr_mean_citedness alt per-paper metric — TOP 6 (note Washington=46 is a flagged data artefact):")
print(oa.sort_values("two_yr_mean_citedness", ascending=False).head(6)[
    ["institution", "two_yr_mean_citedness", "works_count"]].to_string(index=False))

The same universities therefore swing tens of places between systems purely because of what is weighted and whether it is size-normalised — Caltech (small, normalised winner) and Michigan (large, raw-volume winner) are the perfect two-sided illustration.

raw_evidence.label: Scope note for the Analyst — caveats and confounds
raw_evidence.content: Guidance for the analysis. (1) ERA MISMATCH is the dataset's main honest limitation: THE/ARWU/CWUR are 2015, QS is 2023, OpenAlex is current — so a strict 'they disagree' comparison is cleanest on the 2015 trio plus the anchor, treating QS and OpenAlex as recent-state overlays and flagging the mismatch explicitly. (2) The cross-system join is by NORMALISED INSTITUTION NAME (names differ across tables), which produced the 189-institution five-way core; a handful of edge cases may be mis-joined. (3) OpenAlex works_count REWARDS SIZE/AGE and medical output — big, old, hospital-affiliated universities dominate raw volume, so it is a yardstick of quantity, not quality; consider cited_by_count and h_index alongside it, and note that two_yr_mean_citedness has anomalous rows (e.g. Washington ~46 vs peers ~3-7) that look like data artefacts. (4) CWUR indicator columns are RANKS (1 = best), the OPPOSITE direction to the 0-100 scores in THE/ARWU/QS — do not mix them without inverting. (5) The QS 2023 edition uses the PRE-2024 legacy weights (Academic Reputation 40%), not the current formula.

raw_evidence.label: Scope note for the Analyst — caveats and confounds
raw_evidence.content: Guidance for the analysis. (1) ERA MISMATCH is the dataset's main honest limitation: THE/ARWU/CWUR are 2015, QS is 2023, OpenAlex is current — so a strict 'they disagree' comparison is cleanest on the 2015 trio plus the anchor, treating QS and OpenAlex as recent-state overlays and flagging the mismatch explicitly. (2) The cross-system join is by NORMALISED INSTITUTION NAME (names differ across tables), which produced the 189-institution five-way core; a handful of edge cases may be mis-joined. (3) OpenAlex works_count REWARDS SIZE/AGE and medical output — big, old, hospital-affiliated universities dominate raw volume, so it is a yardstick of quantity, not quality; consider cited_by_count and h_index alongside it, and note that two_yr_mean_citedness has anomalous rows (e.g. Washington ~46 vs peers ~3-7) that look like data artefacts. (4) CWUR indicator columns are RANKS (1 = best), the OPPOSITE direction to the 0-100 scores in THE/ARWU/QS — do not mix them without inverting. (5) The QS 2023 edition uses the PRE-2024 legacy weights (Academic Reputation 40%), not the current formula.

raw_evidence.label: Controversy — methodology changes cause artificial volatility
raw_evidence.content: A university can jump or plunge dozens of places without changing at all, simply because a ranker changes its formula. QS's 2024 edition made what it called its largest-ever methodological change, adding three new indicators each worth 5% — International Research Network, Employment Outcomes and Sustainability — and rebalancing the surveys (Academic Reputation cut from 40% to 30%). Analysts noted this made year-on-year comparison essentially apples-to-oranges, and whole national systems moved (many Korean institutions fell under the new weights). This is a direct interpretive hook: the disagreement between systems is compounded by disagreement of each system WITH ITSELF over time, so a headline rank is a snapshot of a methodology, not a fixed truth.

raw_evidence.label: Controversy — rankings can be gamed with bad data
raw_evidence.content: Because several ranking indicators rely on self-reported institutional data, they can be manipulated. In 2022 Columbia University — ranked #2 by U.S. News — was found by its own mathematics professor Michael Thaddeus to have submitted inaccurate figures (class sizes, share of full-time faculty with terminal degrees, instructional spending). When corrected, Columbia fell from #2 to #18, one of the sharpest drops in the ranking's history; the university then withdrew from the undergraduate rankings and later reportedly settled related litigation for about $9 million. Although U.S. News is not one of the four systems in this dataset, the episode is the canonical warning that a headline rank is only as trustworthy as the data feeding it — reinforcing why an independent, non-submitted anchor like OpenAlex matters.

raw_evidence.label: Controversy — methodology changes cause artificial volatility
raw_evidence.content: A university can jump or plunge dozens of places without changing at all, simply because a ranker changes its formula. QS's 2024 edition made what it called its largest-ever methodological change, adding three new indicators each worth 5% — International Research Network, Employment Outcomes and Sustainability — and rebalancing the surveys (Academic Reputation cut from 40% to 30%). Analysts noted this made year-on-year comparison essentially apples-to-oranges, and whole national systems moved (many Korean institutions fell under the new weights). This is a direct interpretive hook: the disagreement between systems is compounded by disagreement of each system WITH ITSELF over time, so a headline rank is a snapshot of a methodology, not a fixed truth.

raw_evidence.label: Controversy — rankings can be gamed with bad data
raw_evidence.content: Because several ranking indicators rely on self-reported institutional data, they can be manipulated. In 2022 Columbia University — ranked #2 by U.S. News — was found by its own mathematics professor Michael Thaddeus to have submitted inaccurate figures (class sizes, share of full-time faculty with terminal degrees, instructional spending). When corrected, Columbia fell from #2 to #18, one of the sharpest drops in the ranking's history; the university then withdrew from the undergraduate rankings and later reportedly settled related litigation for about $9 million. Although U.S. News is not one of the four systems in this dataset, the episode is the canonical warning that a headline rank is only as trustworthy as the data feeding it — reinforcing why an independent, non-submitted anchor like OpenAlex matters.

raw_evidence.label: Controversy — top schools are boycotting the rankings
raw_evidence.content: Institutions themselves increasingly reject the tables' authority. In 2023, led by Yale and Harvard law schools, dozens of top U.S. law schools and several medical schools boycotted the U.S. News rankings, refusing to supply data. Their objections go to methodology: Yale's dean argued the heavily weighted standardised-test metric penalises promising students who cannot afford test prep, Stanford's dean said the formula 'inappropriately discourages public service', and medical deans said the rankings 'measure the wrong things'. U.S. News responded by revising its formula to de-emphasise reputational surveys in favour of outcome measures. The revolt underscores the story's thesis: even the ranked elite dispute that a single weighting captures 'quality'.

raw_evidence.label: Why it matters — rankings steer real decisions
raw_evidence.content: These tables are not academic parlour games; they move students, money and policy. In QS's own International Student Survey, roughly a quarter of prospective students (23.5%) said institutional ranking was the single most important factor in choosing a university and subject, and about a fifth (19.6%) said rankings shaped which COUNTRY they studied in. Ellen Hazelkorn's landmark work documents how rankings now reshape decisions not just for students and parents but for governments, funding agencies, employers and universities' own strategies — a 'global reputation race' in which a few weighting choices by three or four private companies ripple into national policy and billions in tuition and research funding. That stakes-per-decision is exactly why the disagreement between the tables is worth exposing.

raw_evidence.content: The centrepiece client model. Each of the 218 common-core universities carries five REAL 0-100 pillars — rep (QS Academic Reputation survey), cite (THE field-normalised citation impact), teach (THE teaching), intl (THE international outlook), vol (OpenAlex raw output scaled 0-100). A pure-JS function blends them under reader-set weights and re-ranks. Just moving between five preset weightings produces THREE different #1s: balanced weights crown Oxford (87.02), a QS-like reputation-heavy weighting crowns MIT (96.25), and an output-only weighting crowns Michigan (100.0). A THE-like blend also gives MIT; an ARWU-like output blend gives Michigan. The reader discovers first-hand that 'best university' is a slider position, not a fact. Verified identical in Python and Node (code/client_model.js).

raw_evidence.label: Cross-system name join sizes — 218-institution 5-way core
raw_evidence.content: A normalized-name join (code/common.py: lowercase, strip parentheticals/'university'/'the'/'of', de-accent, plus a small alias map for Ann-Arbor/ETH/EPFL variants) reproduces the dataset's advertised common core. Pairwise overlaps: THE n ARWU 297, THE n CWUR 354, THE n QS 306, THE n OpenAlex 280, ARWU n CWUR 439, CWUR n QS 587 (largest), QS n OpenAlex 453. The 2015 trio (THE n ARWU n CWUR) is 285; adding QS gives a 238-school 4-commercial core; adding OpenAlex gives the 218-institution FIVE-WAY common core. That 218 is slightly larger than the README's stated ~189 because this normalizer recovers more true variants (Michigan-Ann Arbor, ETH Zurich, University College London); the exact count is normalizer-dependent, so treat ~200 as the scale, not a precise constant.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_03: join sizes — pairwise, 4-commercial, 5-way core, 2015 trio ---
print("=== ana_03 ===")
print("Per-system distinct normalized institutions after dedup:",
      dict(THE=len(kt), ARWU=len(ka), CWUR=len(kc), QS=len(kq), OpenAlex=len(ko)))
pairs = {
    ("THE", "ARWU"): kt & ka, ("THE", "CWUR"): kt & kc, ("THE", "QS"): kt & kq,
    ("THE", "OpenAlex"): kt & ko, ("ARWU", "CWUR"): ka & kc, ("ARWU", "QS"): ka & kq,
    ("ARWU", "OpenAlex"): ka & ko, ("CWUR", "QS"): kc & kq, ("CWUR", "OpenAlex"): kc & ko,
    ("QS", "OpenAlex"): kq & ko,
}
print("Pairwise overlap (# universities present in BOTH):")
for (a, b), s in pairs.items():
    print(f"  {a} n {b} = {len(s)}")
trio = kt & ka & kc                    # THE 2015 n ARWU 2015 n CWUR 2015
four_commercial = kt & ka & kc & kq    # + QS 2023
core5 = kt & ka & kc & kq & ko         # + OpenAlex
print("2015 trio (THE n ARWU n CWUR):", len(trio))
print("4-commercial core (+QS):", len(four_commercial))
print("5-WAY COMMON CORE (+OpenAlex):", len(core5))

# how many of each system's own top-100 survive into the 5-way core (join coverage)
def top_cover(df, n=100):
    top = set(df.sort_values("rank_num").head(n).key)
    return len(top & core5)
